content: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA) is a medical condition characterized by shortness of breath triggered by sustained aerobic exercise. In individuals with bronchial hyperresponsiveness, intense physical activity can provoke acute narrowing of the airways, which is often assessed by measuring the number of eosinophils in sputum. While EIA shares many clinical features with other forms of asthma and responds to some standard asthma medications, it does not appear to be caused by the same underlying inflammatory mechanisms. The pathophysiology of EIA remains poorly understood. EIA typically manifests after several minutes of vigorous aerobic activity, during which normal nasal breathing is supplemented by mouth breathing. This results in the inhalation of air that is not adequately warmed or humidified by the nasal passages. Consequently, there is increased blood flow to the bronchial tree linings, leading to edema and subsequent constriction of the bronchial vessels, which exacerbates airflow obstruction. This sequence of events produces symptoms similar to those seen in other types of asthma but occurs without the inflammatory changes typically associated with asthma. The prevalence of EIA in the general population is estimated to be between 7% and 20%. Among individuals with symptomatic asthma, the majority exhibit some degree of exercise-induced asthma. Diagnosis History and Symptoms Initial bronchodilation occurs approximately 6–8 minutes after exercise, followed by bronchospasm, which typically resolves within an hour. During this one-hour period, resuming exercise is likely to produce either no symptoms or only mild symptoms. A refractory period often follows the resolution of an attack, likely due to the release of inhibitory prostaglandins, such as prostaglandin E2. Approximately 6–10 hours after an initial attack, a rebound attack with milder symptoms may occur, even without further exertion. This can sometimes be fatal, particularly in scenarios such as walking uphill alongside slow-moving traffic at dusk. Common symptoms include: Shortness of breath Cough Wheezing Altered mental status in severe attacks Physical Examination Vital Signs Tachypnea (rapid breathing) Tachycardia (elevated heart rate) HEENT (Head, Eyes, Ears, Nose, Throat) Cyanosis (bluish discoloration of the skin) secondary to severe hypoxia Lungs High-pitched, prolonged expiratory wheezing, which may be audible even without a stethoscope Other Diagnostic Studies Exercise Challenge Test The exercise challenge test is a direct method to confirm the diagnosis of EIA. A positive test is defined as a 10% reduction in FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in one second) following 6–8 minutes of treadmill exercise. In athletes, documenting airway narrowing in response to exercise aids in the diagnosis and management of asthma. This provides evidence of bronchial hyperresponsiveness, which typically responds to treatment with inhaled corticosteroids and is associated with a reduction in respiratory symptoms during exercise. Treatment Medical Therapy The primary goal of therapy in EIA is to ensure that exercise is not avoided. For athletes who wish to continue their sport, even in adverse conditions, preventive measures such as modified training techniques and medications can be employed. Some athletes utilize the refractory period by deliberately inducing an attack during a warm-up and timing their competition to occur during this period. Stepwise training, involving stages of increasing intensity, can also exploit the refractory period to achieve a full workload. Therapy should be routinely monitored by assessing peak expiratory flow rate before and after exercise. A methacholine challenge test is another option to objectively evaluate the response to therapy. Fish oil supplementation may represent a potentially beneficial non-pharmacologic intervention for patients with EIA. The most common pharmacologic approach involves using a beta-agonist approximately 20 minutes before exercise. Equally effective doses of bronchodilators such as salmeterol, formoterol, and terbutaline have demonstrated short-term protective effects against exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Tachyphylaxis (a reduced response to medication over time) can develop with longand short-acting beta-2 agonists, making them less effective for EIA when used chronically. However, they remain highly effective in preventing bronchospasm when administered immediately before exercise. Nedocromil and cromolyn, delivered via pressurized aerosol, have shown equal efficacy in protecting against EIA in children. A small randomized study demonstrated the additive effects of combining cromolyn with a beta-2 agonist, which may be indicated for high-performance athletes. Nedocromil sodium, when used before exercise, has been shown to reduce the severity and duration of exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. Inhaled corticosteroids, when used for weeks or months before exercise, significantly attenuate exercise-induced bronchoconstriction. However, they do not provide short-term benefits. Montelukast has demonstrated significant protection against EIA and reduces the urinary excretion of leukotrienes commonly observed after exercise. However, leukotriene inhibitors are not effective in all patients with EIA. Other pharmacologic agents hypothesized to provide therapeutic benefits in EIA include furosemide, prostaglandin E2, indomethacin, and heparin. With a combination of the above treatments, the prognosis for EIA is generally very good. Notable athletes, including Olympic swimmers Tom Dolan, Amy Van Dyken, and Nancy Hogshead, baseball Hall of Famer Catfish Hunter, and football player Jerome Bettis, have successfully managed EIA. However, it is worth noting that, according to International Olympic Committee statistics, between one-third and two-thirds of athletes in recent Olympic Games have reported having asthma. Some medical experts suggest that these high rates may be linked to athletes' desire to use complex medications to enhance performance. Future or Investigational Therapies A randomized crossover study compared oral montelukast with inhaled salmeterol, both administered two hours before exercise. Both drugs provided similar benefits, but montelukast's effects lasted 24 hours. In a large randomized study in children, monotherapy with montelukast and combination therapy with montelukast and budesonide yielded better results compared to budesonide monotherapy or combination therapy with budesonide and formoterol.
